key: He who has in himself abundantly the attributes (of the Tao) is like an infant. Poisonous insects will not sting him; fierce beasts will not seize him; birds of prey will not strike him.
s: The chapter opens here, before the infant’s weak bones, firm grip and tireless crying; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 55, reads it as the spirits guarding one who holds virtue as parents guard a newborn, which harms nothing and is harmed by nothing.
src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 55, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 1552800 (2019)

evidence.words: 神明保佑含德之人，若父母之於赤子也。…赤子不害於物，物亦不害之。
evidence.gloss: The spirits protect and aid the person who holds virtue, as father and mother do an infant. … The infant does no harm to things, and things in turn do no harm to it.
evidence.licence: public domain text; transcription CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource)

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref and at match). The Heshang Gong commentary glosses the same lines (比於赤子; 毒蟲不螫; 猛獸不據，玃鳥不搏): spirits guard the one who holds virtue as parents guard an infant, and the infant harms nothing and nothing harms it; the reading carries exactly that. One change to the plain sense: "the newborn’s soft bones" became "the infant’s weak bones", since the chapter has the bones weak and the sinews soft (and says infant). entry-check ok.
